# 14 Temperance ✅️

## 1. Imagery Explained

## 2. Symbol Analysis

**1. The Spiritual Number 14:**

In numerology, 14: 1 + 4 = 5.

4 represents reality, order, and the foundation of the material world.

After the intense transformation of the Death card numbered 13, one needs to come back down to earth—to regain the structure of life, responsibilities, and the rhythm of daily routine. This is the meaning of “4”: stability, reliability, and tangibility.

1 is the new will, the power of active creation, the new direction sprouting after transformation.

1 + 4 = 5 is not a simple addition but a kind of harmony.

Just like the angel on the card, who slowly pours water from one cup into another—

On one side is the personal desire, impulse, and ideal of 1,

On the other side are the social rules, realistic limitations, and collective rhythm of 4.

True wisdom is not about choosing one side but about letting both flow, ultimately forming a dynamic balance—that is what 5 symbolizes: new freedom, new rules, a new middle way.

![Tarot illustration](https://internal-api-drive-stream.feishu.cn/space/api/box/stream/download/authcode/?code=MTY2ZDNiOTc5ODBlNzM3OGMxMWRlZTBkZTA4OTMwNTFfOWZiNTFkNDM3YWQzNzhmMDE0MjZiMmM4YzRlOTRhOGVfSUQ6NzYxOTIzNDIzNjAyOTM0MDYxMl8xNzgyMTgxNDQwOjE3ODIyNjc4NDBfVjM)

In mystical traditions, 14 itself is an alchemical number.

It stands between the destruction of the Death card 13 and the temptation of the Devil card 15, like a buffer zone teaching how to rebuild order after chaos and stay clear-headed before desire.

Its task is to slowly refine “lead”—the coarse desires, instincts, and obsessions—into “gold”: high purity, temperance, and wisdom.

This aligns with the Chinese concept of “Zhong Yong” (the Doctrine of the Mean).

Confucius said: “Be joyful without excess, be sorrowful without harm.”

It’s not about suppressing emotions nor indulging feelings, but walking the middle path just right.

The Temperance card embodies this: no excess, no deficiency, no extremism, no avoidance—finding a third way between two poles.

The angel on the card has one foot in the water and one foot on the ground. Water represents the subconscious, emotions, and spirituality; earth represents reality, logic, and materiality.

He is neither standing on the shore watching nor sinking lost in the water, but firmly building a bridge.

14 = 7 x 2

7 in many traditions represents spiritual pursuit and inner exploration; 2 symbolizes duality, opposition, and choice.

14 means you must coordinate between two “7s”—for example, reason and intuition, body and soul, individual and collective.

It’s not either-or, but letting them nourish each other, becoming a bridge to higher integration.

**2. Belongs to the Fire Element**

The Temperance card belongs to the fire element—not the flame that burns everything down, but the inner spiritual fire—a yearning upwards.

On the angel’s chest, the triangle of “fire” is surrounded by the square of “earth,” a metaphor for spirit guiding matter.

True balance is never stillness but harmony maintained in flow—like the angel pouring water continuously, a cycle that itself embodies vitality.

**3. Astrological Correspondence: Sagittarius**

In astrology, Temperance corresponds to Sagittarius, ruled by Jupiter.

The iris flower on the card corresponds to Sagittarius. Sagittarius has a free soul, loves wandering and traveling, and has no fixed abode, which fits Temperance’s themes of long journeys, business trips, and foreign lands.

**4. Hebrew Letter: Samekh (ס)**

Behind the card is the Kabbalistic letter Samekh (ס), originally meaning “tent peg”—supporting a shelter in the desert.

“No matter how turbulent the world, as long as there is an inner support point, one can be stable.”

Samekh (ס) is shaped like a circle, symbolizing cycles, wholeness, and endless life.

This fits Temperance perfectly: not resisting change nor drifting with the flow, but finding one’s own rhythm in eternal movement.

## 3. Case Studies

### The Core Idea of Temperance—“Learning by Doing”

The angel on the Temperance card says nothing, silently pouring water from one cup to another—

Not fantasizing about balance, but harmonizing in flow;

Not pursuing perfection, but repeatedly pouring to settle impurities and refine essence.

“Learning by doing” means the same: knowledge is not in books but in your hands;

Ability does not come from plans but grows through trial, error, repetition, and adjustment.

Both reject armchair theorizing, believing true insight happens in the muddy reality of the real world.

Who best embodies the Temperance card?

Xu Sanduo.

He has no talent—poor physical fitness, slow reactions, awkward speech;

But he believes a simple phrase: “Doing meaningful things is living well.”

So when others practice marching a hundred times, he practices three hundred;

When others stop at their pull-up limit, he grits his teeth and does one more;

When no one repairs the road, he lays stones alone;

When the team disbands, he still guards his post.

He doesn’t learn first then act, but learns while acting—

This is the true form of “learning by doing”: clumsy, repetitive, full of failure, yet incredibly solid.

Temperance teaches finding the middle way amid extremes.

Xu Sanduo precisely finds his balance between “foolishness” and “tenacity,” “obedience” and “autonomy,” “meaninglessness” and “meaning.”

He is like that angel, one foot on the desolate reality of the grassland’s fifth squad, one foot on the ideal of “never abandon, never give up,”

His hands never stop pouring water—turning action into practice, persistence into character.

When the TV series *Soldier Assault* aired, “Xu Sanduo” became a symbol of the era.

“Never abandon, never give up” was written into textbooks, shouted in military training, and posted on company walls.

He is not a genius, not a hero, just an ordinary person who earned dignity through “doing.”

And this daily pouring is exactly what makes Temperance so moving: greatness hidden in ordinary repetition.

Some might say Yuan Longping, Ma Long, or Cheng Dongqing also fit,

But they tend to lean toward endurance, willpower, or dreaming—

Only Xu Sanduo’s growth fully depends on “doing,” and the process is filled with clumsiness and trial and error,

This is precisely the truest essence of “learning by doing.”

The angel of Temperance doesn’t preach, just pours water;

Xu Sanduo doesn’t boast, just buries his head and works.

But it is this posture of adjusting in action and refining through repetition

That makes “learning by doing” no longer theory but a life rhythm.

He is not repairing roads, but cultivating character;

He is not practicing pull-ups, but temperance.

True wisdom is not in the clouds but in the moment your hands are covered in dirt and you work hard.
